title: NASA’s Oldest Martian Spacecraft Have Been Running for Decades. Here’s How
gist: NASA's Mars Odyssey (at Mars since 2001) and MRO (20 years) have far outlived design lives thanks to post-1999 over-engineering, redundancy and 'margin' in battery and propellant, plus constant improvisation. Scientists worry NASA's next Mars efforts (a Blue Origin relay-only comms satellite, a small particle-physics mission, and the rapid nuclear-propelled Skyfall helicopters) signal a return to 'faster, cheaper' that will weaken science.

insights.claim: Mars Odyssey and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter were designed to last only a few years but have operated for roughly 25 and 20 years respectively, and are among the most productive spacecraft ever.
insights.speaker: Meghan Bartels
insights.so_what: Upfront investment in robustness can produce extreme lifetime returns on space assets.
insights.quote: Both Odyssey and MRO are some of the most productive spacecraft that have ever existed

insights.claim: NASA's 1999 losses of the Mars Climate Orbiter (an imperial-vs-metric units mix-up) and Mars Polar Lander (an untested software error) led it to invest more in pre-launch testing of every component and configuration for Odyssey and MRO.
insights.speaker: Meghan Bartels
insights.so_what: Costly failures under cost-cutting regimes drive the over-engineering that later yields durable assets.

insights.claim: NASA's principle of 'margin' meant MRO launched with a larger battery and more propellant than strictly needed, and that surplus is now what lets NASA hope to run it for another decade.
insights.speaker: Meghan Bartels
insights.so_what: Spare capacity at launch is the main lever for extending mission life, a design tradeoff relevant to satellite operators.

insights.so_what: Autonomy and redundancy are prerequisites for deep-space hardware, raising cost but enabling longevity.

insights.claim: Skyfall, a trio of small Mars helicopters, is slated to launch aboard the first nuclear-propelled spacecraft within two years, a timeline the author calls shockingly rapid for a mission with limited research value.
